flashcards.question: What is the capture limitation for this course?
flashcards.answer: Several visible exercise/setup/wrap-up pages were video-only or empty; by repo rule they are recorded as out of scope, not blockers.
flashcards.example: A "Set up your AWS account" video lesson with no accompanying transcript text is logged as out of scope rather than left as an unresolved gap.

flashcards.question: Should this course be moved from todo to done now?
flashcards.answer: Yes. Under the video-scope rule, readable non-video sections were captured and video-only sections were recorded as out of scope.
flashcards.example: All readable lesson pages for the Bedrock course are captured while two video-only demo segments stay marked out of scope, so the course moves to done.

flashcards.question: How should AWS-specific Bedrock setup details be treated for the certification?
flashcards.answer: As context only; the exam guide marks specific cloud provider configurations out of scope.
flashcards.example: Knowing that Bedrock requires enabling model access in the AWS console is useful background, but the exam will not test the exact console click path.

flashcards.question: What three tradeoffs drive Claude model selection in the course?
flashcards.answer: Intelligence, speed/latency, and cost.
flashcards.example: A team picks a smaller, faster model for real-time chat autocomplete but a larger model for overnight batch summarization where latency matters less.

flashcards.question: When should a stronger, slower, more expensive model be selected?
flashcards.answer: When the task requires deeper reasoning and the outcome justifies the added latency and cost.
flashcards.example: A legal-contract risk analysis tool uses the strongest model because a missed clause is costlier than the extra few seconds and cents per call.

flashcards.question: Why might one application use multiple model tiers?
flashcards.answer: Different subtasks can optimize for speed, cost, or reasoning depth independently.
flashcards.example: A support app uses a fast, cheap model to classify ticket urgency and a stronger model only for drafting the final customer reply.

flashcards.question: Who manages conversation history in a Bedrock/Claude chat app?
flashcards.answer: The application manages and resends the relevant message history.
flashcards.example: A chatbot backend stores each turn in a database and reassembles the last N messages into the `messages` array on every new Bedrock InvokeModel call.

flashcards.question: What happens if a follow-up request omits prior conversation context?
flashcards.answer: Claude treats it as an independent call and may miss prior facts or intent.
flashcards.example: A user says "make it shorter" in a new request with no history attached, and Claude has no idea what "it" refers to.

flashcards.question: What operational issue can model IDs and regions create?
flashcards.answer: A model may not be available in the selected region, causing brittle deployment behavior.
flashcards.example: An app hardcodes a Claude model ID for us-east-1 and starts throwing errors when traffic is routed through an eu-west-1 Bedrock endpoint where that model isn't enabled.

flashcards.question: What belongs in a system prompt?
flashcards.answer: Durable role, behavior, boundaries, policy, style, and output expectations.
flashcards.example: "You are a customer support agent for Acme; never share internal pricing, always respond in a friendly tone, and cite the relevant help-article ID" belongs in the system prompt.

flashcards.question: Why not put core behavior only in repeated user instructions?
flashcards.answer: It is repetitive, user-visible, and weaker than durable system-level configuration.
flashcards.example: Retyping "always answer in bullet points" at the top of every user message is redundant compared to setting it once in the system prompt.

flashcards.question: When should temperature generally be low?
flashcards.answer: For extraction, grading, production workflows, and repeatable behavior.
flashcards.example: A pipeline that pulls invoice totals into a database field sets temperature near 0 so the same invoice yields the same extracted number every run.

flashcards.question: Does low temperature guarantee correctness?
flashcards.answer: No. It improves repeatability but still needs validation and review.
flashcards.example: A low-temperature extraction run consistently returns the same wrong field mapping, so a validation step is still needed to catch it.

flashcards.question: What problem does streaming solve?
flashcards.answer: It improves perceived latency by returning output incrementally.
flashcards.example: A chat UI shows Claude's response appearing word by word instead of the user staring at a blank screen for ten seconds before the full answer appears.

flashcards.question: What problem does streaming not solve?
flashcards.answer: It does not enforce schema, correctness, or semantic validation.
flashcards.example: Streaming a JSON response token by token still lets the final output be malformed or missing a required field.

flashcards.question: What can prefilled assistant messages do?
flashcards.answer: Steer the beginning and shape of Claude's response.
flashcards.example: Prefilling the assistant turn with "{" pushes Claude straight into producing a JSON object instead of a prose lead-in.

flashcards.question: What do stop sequences do?
flashcards.answer: Stop generation at predefined boundaries.
flashcards.example: Setting a stop sequence of "\`\`\`" halts generation right after a code block closes, trimming trailing commentary.

flashcards.question: When are prefill and stop sequences useful for structured output?
flashcards.answer: For lower-risk cases where raw JSON/code needs less surrounding prose.
flashcards.example: A quick internal script prefills "{" and stops at "}" to grab a small config object without building a full tool schema.

flashcards.question: What is stronger than asking Claude to return JSON?
flashcards.answer: Tool-based structured output with a schema plus validation.
flashcards.example: Defining a `record_order` tool with a JSON schema for `order_id`, `total`, and `items` guarantees Claude's output matches that shape, unlike asking it to "return JSON" in prose.

flashcards.question: Why can schema-valid output still need validation?
flashcards.answer: It can contain semantic errors, unsupported values, or wrong field assignments.
flashcards.example: A tool call correctly fills the `status` field with a valid enum value, but picks "shipped" for an order that hasn't actually shipped yet.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between prompt engineering and prompt evaluation?
flashcards.answer: Engineering improves prompts; evaluation measures whether they work.
flashcards.example: Rewriting a summarization prompt to add constraints is prompt engineering; running it against 50 labeled test articles and scoring accuracy is prompt evaluation.

flashcards.question: What are the core pieces of an eval workflow?
flashcards.answer: Prompt, evaluation dataset, model output, grader, and iteration.
flashcards.example: A team tests a classification prompt against 100 labeled emails, scores each output with a grader, then tweaks the prompt and reruns the same dataset.

flashcards.question: When is a code-based grader best?
flashcards.answer: When correctness can be checked deterministically, such as syntax, JSON validity, or required fields.
flashcards.example: A script runs `json.loads()` on every model output and flags a failure whenever parsing throws or a required "id" field is missing.

flashcards.question: When is a model-based grader useful?
flashcards.answer: When evaluation requires semantic or qualitative judgment.
flashcards.example: A second Claude call is prompted to rate whether a generated customer-support reply is "polite and on-topic" on a 1-5 scale.

flashcards.question: Why should eval datasets include edge cases?
flashcards.answer: Happy-path tests hide failures that appear in production.
flashcards.example: A dataset that only includes well-formatted invoices misses how the prompt handles a scanned invoice with a smudged total, which shows up once deployed.

flashcards.question: What is the first prompt-engineering improvement for vague output?
flashcards.answer: Lead with a clear, direct statement of the task.
flashcards.example: Replacing "Can you maybe help with this document?" with "Summarize this document in 3 bullet points" removes the vagueness up front.

flashcards.question: What should specificity add to a prompt?
flashcards.answer: Criteria, constraints, process steps, and desired output properties.
flashcards.example: "Summarize in exactly 3 bullets, under 15 words each, focusing only on financial figures" gives Claude concrete criteria instead of a vague "summarize this."

flashcards.question: Why use XML tags in prompts?
flashcards.answer: They separate instructions, examples, context, and output sections clearly.
flashcards.example: Wrapping the source document in `<document>...</document>` and the task instructions in `<instructions>...</instructions>` keeps Claude from confusing the two.

flashcards.question: What do few-shot examples teach?
flashcards.answer: Output format and judgment for ambiguous cases.
flashcards.example: Showing two example support tickets labeled "urgent" and "not urgent" teaches Claude how to classify a borderline third ticket the same way.

flashcards.question: Where can good few-shot examples come from?
flashcards.answer: Evaluation failures and representative edge cases.
flashcards.example: A ticket that the model previously misclassified during eval testing gets added as a labeled few-shot example so the same mistake doesn't repeat.

flashcards.question: What is the basic tool-use loop?
flashcards.answer: Send tools, inspect `tool_use`, execute the tool, return `tool_result`, and continue.
flashcards.example: Claude emits a `tool_use` block calling `get_weather(city="Austin")`, the app runs that function, sends back a `tool_result` with the temperature, and Claude uses it to answer the user.

flashcards.question: Why should applications inspect `stop_reason`?
flashcards.answer: It tells whether Claude is requesting tools or producing a final answer.
flashcards.example: An app checks `stop_reason == "tool_use"` to decide whether to run a function versus `stop_reason == "end_turn"` to display the reply straight to the user.

flashcards.question: Why must tool results be added to conversation history?
flashcards.answer: Claude needs the results in context to reason about the next step.
flashcards.example: After a `search_orders` tool returns a list of order IDs, that `tool_result` is appended to the conversation so Claude can pick the right one for the next step.

flashcards.question: What makes a tool description effective?
flashcards.answer: Clear purpose, inputs, outputs, boundaries, and when to use it versus similar tools.
flashcards.example: "Use `search_orders` to find orders by customer email; use `get_order` only when you already have a specific order ID" tells Claude exactly when each tool applies.

flashcards.question: Why should tools be narrow and scoped?
flashcards.answer: Focused tools reduce selection ambiguity and misuse.
flashcards.example: Splitting a bloated `manage_orders` tool into separate `get_order`, `cancel_order`, and `refund_order` tools makes it clearer which one Claude should call for a refund request.

flashcards.question: What does a JSON schema tell Claude?
flashcards.answer: The tool arguments, required fields, allowed structure, and field meanings.
flashcards.example: A schema marking `email` as a required string and `priority` as an enum of "low"/"medium"/"high" tells Claude exactly what shape to fill in for a `create_ticket` call.

flashcards.question: What does `tool_choice: auto` mean?
flashcards.answer: Claude may call a tool or answer directly.
flashcards.example: Asked "what's 2+2?" with a calculator tool available under `tool_choice: auto`, Claude just answers "4" directly instead of invoking the tool.

flashcards.question: What does `tool_choice: any` mean?
flashcards.answer: Claude must call a tool but can choose which one.
flashcards.example: With `tool_choice: any` and both `search_orders` and `get_order` available, Claude picks whichever tool fits the request but cannot just reply in plain text.

flashcards.question: When should forced tool choice be used?
flashcards.answer: When a specific tool must run first or when testing a required tool path.
flashcards.example: A test harness forces `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "lookup_customer"}` to verify the tool integration works before letting Claude choose freely.

flashcards.question: When is batch tool use appropriate?
flashcards.answer: When multiple independent operations can be executed in parallel.
flashcards.example: Claude issues three separate `get_weather` calls for New York, London, and Tokyo in one turn since none of the calls depend on another's result.

flashcards.question: What is the risk of batching dependent operations?
flashcards.answer: It hides ordering requirements and can produce incorrect workflow behavior.
flashcards.example: Batching a `create_account` call together with a `create_order` call for that same account can fail if the order call runs before the account exists.

flashcards.question: Why is tool-based extraction more reliable than text JSON?
flashcards.answer: Claude fills structured tool inputs instead of free-form prose.
flashcards.example: A `record_contact` tool with typed `name` and `phone` fields reliably produces a clean structured record instead of Claude writing "Name: John, Phone: 555-1234" as text to be re-parsed.

flashcards.question: What is the tradeoff of a generic `to_json` extraction tool?
flashcards.answer: Less schema work, but weaker guarantees than a purpose-built schema.
flashcards.example: A generic `to_json` tool can quickly extract "any relevant fields" from a messy email, but won't guarantee a `phone_number` field is always present the way a dedicated schema would.

flashcards.question: What is the transferable exam lesson from the Bedrock text editor tool?
flashcards.answer: Pick specialized read/edit tools by task shape and inspect context before modifying files.
flashcards.example: Before replacing a line in a config file, the text editor tool first reads the surrounding lines so the edit targets the correct occurrence rather than guessing blindly.

flashcards.question: What is the purpose of RAG?
flashcards.answer: Retrieve relevant source chunks instead of sending entire large documents.
flashcards.example: Instead of pasting an entire 500-page policy manual into the prompt, a RAG system retrieves only the 3 paragraphs about vacation accrual to answer a specific employee question.

flashcards.question: Why does chunking strategy matter?
flashcards.answer: Chunks determine whether retrieved context is relevant and coherent.
flashcards.example: Splitting a contract mid-sentence at a fixed character count can cut off the clause that answers the question, while splitting by section keeps it intact.

flashcards.question: What is size-based chunking best for?
flashcards.answer: Simple implementation when document structure is weak or unavailable.
flashcards.example: A folder of unformatted plain-text chat logs is split into fixed 500-character chunks since there are no headings or sections to key off of.

flashcards.question: What is structure-based chunking best for?
flashcards.answer: Preserving meaningful sections like headings, records, or document units.
flashcards.example: A markdown handbook is chunked by `##` heading so each retrieved chunk is a complete, self-contained policy section rather than a fragment.

flashcards.question: What are embeddings useful for?
flashcards.answer: Semantic search based on meaning rather than exact word matching.
flashcards.example: A search for "how do I get my money back" retrieves a chunk titled "Refund Policy" even though none of those exact words appear together in the query.

flashcards.question: When is BM25 stronger than embeddings?
flashcards.answer: Exact identifiers, names, codes, policy terms, filenames, and incident numbers.
flashcards.example: A search for the exact ticket ID "INC-004521" is matched reliably by BM25's keyword overlap, whereas an embedding search might return semantically similar but wrong incident tickets.

flashcards.question: Why combine embeddings and BM25?
flashcards.answer: To capture both semantic similarity and exact-term matches.
flashcards.example: A hybrid search for "billing error on invoice INV-9981" uses embeddings to find billing-related content and BM25 to make sure the exact invoice number surfaces.

flashcards.question: What does reranking do in RAG?
flashcards.answer: Reorders retrieved chunks by relevance to the specific question.
flashcards.example: An initial retrieval pulls 20 loosely related chunks, and a reranker moves the 3 chunks that most directly answer "what is the cancellation deadline" to the top.

flashcards.question: Why add context to chunks before indexing?
flashcards.answer: It helps isolated chunks retain enough source meaning when retrieved later.
flashcards.example: A chunk that just says "the deadline is 30 days" gets prefixed with "This is from the Refund Policy section on returns:" so it still makes sense retrieved on its own.

flashcards.question: Why do citations matter in Claude document workflows?
flashcards.answer: They preserve evidence so users can verify where claims came from.
flashcards.example: A generated answer states "your warranty expires in 2027" with a citation pointing to page 4 of the uploaded warranty PDF, letting the user check the source directly.

flashcards.question: When is prompt caching useful?
flashcards.answer: When large stable prompt prefixes repeat within the cache window.
flashcards.example: A 10,000-token system prompt with tool definitions is cached so each new user turn only pays for the small delta instead of re-processing the whole prefix.

flashcards.question: Is prompt caching a reliability feature?
flashcards.answer: No. It helps cost/latency, not correctness.
flashcards.example: Caching a flawed system prompt makes every subsequent call cheaper and faster, but it still reproduces the same flawed behavior each time.

flashcards.question: When should extended thinking be used?
flashcards.answer: For complex reasoning where quality justifies extra latency and cost.
flashcards.example: A multi-step math word problem or a tricky debugging task benefits from extended thinking, while a simple "translate this sentence" request does not need it.

flashcards.question: What are the three core MCP server primitives?
flashcards.answer: Tools, resources, and prompts.
flashcards.example: A GitHub MCP server might expose a `create_issue` tool, a `repo://readme` resource, and a "summarize pull request" prompt template.

flashcards.question: Who controls MCP tools?
flashcards.answer: The model controls tool use.
flashcards.example: Claude decides on its own, mid-conversation, to call an MCP `search_files` tool when it determines it needs to look something up.

flashcards.question: Who controls MCP resources?
flashcards.answer: The application controls when resources are read and included.
flashcards.example: A code-editor plugin decides to attach the `file://current_file.py` resource to the context only when the user has that file open.

flashcards.question: Who controls MCP prompts?
flashcards.answer: Users or client workflows intentionally invoke them.
flashcards.example: A user explicitly selects a "/summarize-pr" MCP prompt template from a menu rather than Claude deciding on its own to run it.

flashcards.question: When should an MCP capability be a tool?
flashcards.answer: When Claude should take an action or call an external capability.
flashcards.example: "Send a Slack message" or "create a Jira ticket" are actions, so they belong as MCP tools rather than resources.

flashcards.question: When should an MCP capability be a resource?
flashcards.answer: When it exposes read-only context or catalogs for the app to include.
flashcards.example: A catalog of available product SKUs is exposed as an MCP resource the app attaches to context, rather than a tool Claude has to call and wait on.

flashcards.question: What is the MCP inspector for?
flashcards.answer: Testing and debugging MCP server primitives before production use.
flashcards.example: A developer uses the MCP inspector to manually invoke a new `get_invoice` tool and check its response shape before wiring it into a live agent.

flashcards.question: What does `/init` do in Claude Code?
flashcards.answer: It inspects the project and creates project context in `CLAUDE.md`.
flashcards.example: Running `/init` in a new Next.js repo scans the folder structure and package.json, then writes a `CLAUDE.md` noting it's a Next.js app with a `components/` and `api/` layout.

flashcards.question: When is a planning-first Claude Code workflow best?
flashcards.answer: Before risky or multi-file changes with design tradeoffs.
flashcards.example: Before migrating an app's auth system to a new provider, a plan is written and reviewed first rather than jumping straight into editing a dozen files.

flashcards.question: Why is test-driven iteration effective with Claude Code?
flashcards.answer: Failing tests provide concrete feedback for implementation refinement.
flashcards.example: Claude writes a test asserting `parse_date("2026-09-03")` returns the right object, watches it fail, then iterates on the implementation until it passes.

flashcards.question: Why connect MCP servers to Claude Code?
flashcards.answer: To add team-specific tools, resources, and prompts to development workflows.
flashcards.example: A team connects an internal Jira MCP server so Claude Code can create and update tickets directly as part of a coding session.

flashcards.question: Why use git worktrees for parallel Claude Code?
flashcards.answer: They isolate file edits so concurrent agents do not collide.
flashcards.example: Two agents work on separate git worktrees, one fixing a bug in `auth.py` and another adding a feature in `billing.py`, without either touching the other's working copy.

flashcards.question: What must happen before merging parallel Claude Code work?
flashcards.answer: Review diffs, run tests, and resolve conflicts deliberately.
flashcards.example: Before merging two worktree branches, the developer reads each diff, runs the full test suite, and manually resolves a conflict where both branches edited the same config file.

flashcards.question: What pattern did the course emphasize for effective agents?
flashcards.answer: Observe the environment first, then act with focused tools and evaluate results.
flashcards.example: Before renaming a function, an agent first searches the codebase for all its call sites, then makes the edits, then runs tests to confirm nothing broke.

flashcards.question: Why should agents have focused tool sets?
flashcards.answer: Fewer relevant tools improve selection reliability.
flashcards.example: A coding agent given only `read_file`, `edit_file`, and `run_tests` picks the right tool more reliably than one also cluttered with unrelated marketing or billing tools.

flashcards.question: What tasks are best suited to agents?
flashcards.answer: High-value tasks where the cost of occasional errors can be controlled.
flashcards.example: An agent triages and drafts replies to routine support tickets with human review before sending, since a wrong draft is cheap to catch and fix.

flashcards.question: How should computer use lessons be studied for this exam?
flashcards.answer: Keep only the general tool-loop idea; computer use itself is out of scope.
flashcards.example: Remember that computer use follows the same observe-act-evaluate loop as other tool use, but skip memorizing the specific screenshot/click coordinate mechanics for the exam.

practice_questions.scenario: A team is building a customer-facing assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Most requests are simple account questions, but 8% require multi-step reasoning over policy, order history, and exception handling. The team proposes using the most capable model for every request to maximize quality.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best architecture decision?

choices.text: Use the most capable model for every request because quality always matters more than latency.
Use the fastest model for every request because customer-facing applications should always optimize latency.
Route simple requests to a faster/lower-cost model and reserve stronger models for complex reasoning cases.
Randomly split traffic across all available models and choose the one with the lowest average cost.

practice_questions.explanation: The course frames model selection as a tradeoff among intelligence, speed, and cost. A routed multi-model design lets each subtask use the smallest model that meets quality requirements while preserving stronger reasoning for harder cases.

distractors.A: Overpays in latency and cost for simple cases.
distractors.B: Under-serves complex cases that need stronger reasoning.
distractors.D: Random allocation ignores task requirements and makes quality less predictable.

practice_questions.scenario: A Bedrock chat app answers "What is 1+1?" correctly. The user then asks "And 3 more?" but Claude responds as if it has no prior context.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the root cause?

choices.text: Bedrock and Claude automatically store state, so the model must have selected the wrong tool.
The application failed to resend the relevant conversation history in the follow-up request.
The model needs a higher temperature to remember conversational context.
Streaming must be enabled for multi-turn conversations.

practice_questions.explanation: Claude API calls are stateless from the application perspective. The app must preserve and resend relevant user, assistant, and tool messages.

distractors.A: The course explicitly emphasizes application-managed message history.
distractors.C: Temperature affects sampling, not persistence of prior messages.
distractors.D: Streaming affects response delivery, not memory.

practice_questions.scenario: A workflow generates AWS EventBridge JSON rules. Claude often wraps the JSON in markdown fences and explanatory prose, causing downstream parsing failures. The team wants a quick improvement for a low-risk internal tool.
practice_questions.prompt: Which first change best matches the course material?

choices.text: Use assistant message prefilling plus a stop sequence to steer raw JSON output and trim extra prose.
Increase temperature so Claude explores more output formats.
Add a disclaimer telling users to manually remove markdown before parsing.
Switch to streaming because streamed responses are easier to parse.

practice_questions.explanation: The course shows prefilled assistant messages and stop sequences as direct controls for reducing unwanted wrappers around structured output. For production-grade extraction, tool/schema enforcement and validation would still be stronger.

distractors.B: Higher temperature generally reduces repeatability.
distractors.C: Manual cleanup does not fix the workflow.
distractors.D: Streaming changes delivery timing, not output structure.

practice_questions.scenario: A production extraction system sends Claude's JSON output into a downstream database. The team already uses a prompt that says "return only valid JSON," but occasional malformed or semantically wrong values still slip through.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best exam-oriented improvement?

choices.text: Use a tool with a JSON schema for structured output, then validate the result before writing downstream.
Tell Claude that invalid JSON is not allowed under any circumstances.
Use the same prompt with lower temperature and remove all validators.
Ask users to check the database after each extraction.

practice_questions.explanation: Tool-based structured output improves schema compliance, and validation catches semantic or business-rule errors that schemas alone may not prevent.

distractors.B: Prompt-only enforcement is probabilistic.
distractors.C: Low temperature helps repeatability but does not replace validation.
distractors.D: Manual cleanup after writes is weaker than pre-write validation.

practice_questions.scenario: You are designing a reminder assistant with three possible operations: get the current time, add a duration to a date, and create a reminder. Claude frequently chooses the wrong operation because the tool descriptions are short and similar.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best first fix?

choices.text: Combine all operations into one generic `do_datetime_stuff` tool.
Expand each tool description with purpose, inputs, outputs, boundaries, and examples.
Remove all descriptions so Claude relies only on tool names.
Force the create-reminder tool for every request.

practice_questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are a primary signal for selection. Clear boundaries are especially important when tools are related but not interchangeable.

distractors.A: A generic tool hides intent and creates ambiguous inputs.
distractors.C: Removing descriptions worsens selection reliability.
distractors.D: Forced selection is useful only when a specific required tool must run.

practice_questions.scenario: Claude may answer a user directly or request one or more tools. The current application looks for phrases like "I need to use a tool" in assistant text to decide whether to execute tools.
practice_questions.prompt: What should the application do instead?

choices.text: Inspect response structure and `stop_reason`, execute requested tools, return `tool_result`, and continue until final answer.
Increase max tokens so Claude has enough room to describe tool requests.
Require users to type "tool mode" before asking operational questions.
Execute every available tool on every turn and let Claude choose from the results.

practice_questions.explanation: Reliable tool loops inspect structured tool-use responses and stop reasons rather than parsing natural language hints.

distractors.B: More tokens do not solve control-flow detection.
distractors.C: Users should not manage internal tool modes.
distractors.D: Running every tool wastes resources and pollutes context.

practice_questions.scenario: A RAG system uses only embeddings. It performs well for conceptual questions but fails when users ask about exact incident IDs such as `INC-2023-Q4-011`.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best retrieval improvement?

choices.text: Add lexical search such as BM25 and merge it with embedding results.
Increase the model temperature so it considers more possible chunks.
Remove chunk metadata to reduce prompt size.
Replace all retrieval with a single prompt containing the full document collection.

practice_questions.explanation: Embeddings capture semantic similarity, while BM25 is strong for exact terms, IDs, and names. Hybrid retrieval combines both strengths.

distractors.B: Temperature affects generation, not retrieval matching.
distractors.C: Removing metadata weakens provenance and filtering.
distractors.D: Full-context prompting is often impractical and can degrade attention.

practice_questions.scenario: A document assistant retrieves chunks that contain the right words but lack enough surrounding context to answer accurately. The source document has strong section-level meaning that gets lost when chunks are split.
practice_questions.prompt: Which technique best addresses this?

choices.text: Contextual retrieval: add short source-aware context to chunks before indexing.
Remove section headings so every chunk looks uniform.
Use only size-based chunks with no overlap.
Disable citations to save tokens.

practice_questions.explanation: Contextual retrieval situates each chunk within the larger source before indexing, making retrieved chunks more meaningful in isolation.

distractors.B: Headings often provide important context.
distractors.C: Fixed-size chunks alone may split semantic units.
distractors.D: Citations support trust and do not fix lost context.

practice_questions.scenario: A team is building an MCP server for a document system. They need Claude to edit documents, the application to include selected document contents when users mention them, and users to invoke a tested "convert to markdown" template.
practice_questions.prompt: How should these be modeled?

choices.text: Document editing as a tool, document contents as resources, and markdown conversion as a prompt.
Document editing as a resource, document contents as a prompt, and markdown conversion as a tool.
Make everything a tool because tools are the only MCP primitive Claude can see.
Make everything a prompt because prompts are easier to test.

practice_questions.explanation: MCP tools are model-controlled actions, resources are app-controlled context, and prompts are reusable user/client-invoked templates.

distractors.B: Editing is an action, not read-only context.
distractors.C: MCP also exposes resources and prompts.
distractors.D: Prompts cannot replace actions or context catalogs.

practice_questions.scenario: An engineer writes a new MCP server with read and edit tools. They immediately connect it to Claude Code and ask it to modify project files. The first run fails because the edit tool schema is wrong.
practice_questions.prompt: What should they have done first?

choices.text: Test the MCP server primitives with the inspector before relying on them in a client workflow.
Give Claude Code more tools so it can recover from the bad schema.
Remove schemas from the MCP tools.
Use a user-level server only, because project-level servers cannot be tested.

practice_questions.explanation: The course presents the MCP inspector as a development/debugging tool for validating server behavior before integration.

distractors.B: More tools do not fix a broken interface.
distractors.C: Schemas are part of reliable tool contracts.
distractors.D: Server scope and testability are separate concerns.

practice_questions.scenario: A team wants three Claude Code instances to work on separate improvements at the same time. They plan to run all three in the same checkout to save disk space.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best course-aligned advice?

choices.text: Use separate git worktrees so each instance has an isolated workspace, then review and merge deliberately.
Run all instances in one checkout because Claude Code automatically coordinates file locks.
Disable tests until all three instances finish.
Ask each instance not to edit the same files and trust the instruction.

practice_questions.explanation: The course uses git worktrees to prevent concurrent Claude Code instances from overwriting or conflicting with each other's file changes.

distractors.B: Automatic coordination should not be assumed.
distractors.C: Tests are important verification, not optional cleanup.
distractors.D: Prompt instructions are weaker than workspace isolation.

practice_questions.scenario: A production service sends error logs to Claude, which proposes code fixes automatically. Leadership wants the system to deploy every generated fix immediately.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best reliability critique?

choices.text: Automated debugging can help, but production-affecting fixes need guardrails, tests, review, and controlled deployment.
Immediate deployment is safe because Claude inspected the logs.
The system should use higher temperature to find more creative fixes.
Automated debugging should never be used for production systems.

practice_questions.explanation: The course shows automated debugging as powerful, but the exam rewards reliability judgment: production workflows need verification and human or programmatic controls.

distractors.B: Log inspection alone is insufficient.
distractors.C: More creativity does not improve deployment safety.
distractors.D: The pattern can be useful when constrained and verified.

practice_questions.scenario: A developer asks whether to study the course's computer-use implementation details for the Claude Certified Architect - Foundations exam.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best answer?

choices.text: Study every computer-use limit and API detail because it is a primary exam domain.
Ignore the entire agents section because computer use appears there.
Keep the transferable tool-loop and agent-design lessons, but do not over-study computer use because the exam guide marks it out of scope.
Replace MCP study time with computer-use practice because both involve tools.

distractors.A: Computer use is out of scope.
distractors.B: The agents section contains exam-relevant Claude Code, tool-loop, and agent-quality ideas.
distractors.D: MCP is explicitly in scope and should not be displaced.

practice_questions.scenario: A prompt engineering team keeps improving a meal-plan prompt by intuition. Each iteration sounds better in demos, but regressions appear when users have allergies, unusual goals, or strict constraints.
practice_questions.prompt: What should they add?

choices.text: A repeatable prompt evaluation workflow with representative test cases, graders, and iteration.
More adjectives in the prompt, such as "excellent" and "high quality."
A higher context window so the model sees more examples at once.
Streaming to expose partial results sooner.

practice_questions.explanation: The course emphasizes evaluation as the way to measure prompt quality and catch regressions across representative scenarios.

distractors.B: Vague quality words do not measure behavior.
distractors.C: More context does not replace test coverage.

notes_sections.title: Key Concepts
notes_sections.body:
| Concept | Study Notes |
|---|---|
| Vertex as provider context | The course is framed around calling Claude through Google Cloud Vertex AI. For the certification, keep provider setup as deployment context and focus on transferable Claude architecture, tools, prompts, context, and reliability patterns. |
| Enabling Anthropic models in Vertex | The readable setup lesson directs learners to Vertex AI Model Garden, search for Anthropic, choose the intended model, and enable it if needed. Exam relevance: ensure the deployment environment exposes the model before debugging application logic. |
| `gcloud` authentication | The setup lesson uses `gcloud init`, `gcloud auth login`, project selection, and application-default login so the SDK can use local credentials. Exam relevance: credentials and provider setup are prerequisites, not reliability guarantees. |
| Application-owned API orchestration | A Vertex-hosted Claude call still relies on the application to send messages, manage history, inspect tool-use responses, execute tools, return results, validate outputs, and handle errors. |
| Model selection | Choose the smallest, fastest, lowest-cost model that meets the task's quality bar. Escalate capability for complex reasoning, high ambiguity, or high-value decisions. |
| Multi-turn state | Claude does not magically know prior turns unless the application supplies relevant conversation history. Preserve critical user/assistant/tool messages and trim irrelevant context. |
| System prompts | Use system prompts for durable behavior, role, policy, boundaries, and response requirements. Do not bury transient case facts or business state in the system prompt. |
| Temperature | Lower temperature improves repeatability but does not prove correctness. Use validation, tests, schemas, and review for production reliability. |
| Streaming | Streaming improves perceived latency. It does not solve correctness, schema validity, or tool-loop control. |
| Output control | Prefill and stop sequences can shape low-risk text output, but schema/tool enforcement and validators are stronger for machine-consumed data. |
| Structured data | For extraction or downstream automation, prefer JSON-schema-backed tool use or structured APIs plus semantic validation over plain "return JSON" prompting. |
| Prompt evaluation | Evaluate prompts against representative examples, criteria, and graders. Iterate before scaling to production workloads. |
| Model-based grading | Use a model grader for semantic quality, completeness, and judgment-heavy criteria. Calibrate with examples and human spot checks. |
| Code-based grading | Use deterministic code checks for syntax, parseability, schema validity, exact fields, regexes, arithmetic, and other objective rules. |
| Clear/direct prompting | Put the task and success criteria up front. Ambiguous prompts force Claude to infer intent and reduce consistency. |
| Specific prompting | Add constraints, acceptance criteria, examples, and edge cases when quality depends on judgment. |
| XML tags | Use tags to separate instructions, examples, context, and output requirements when prompts contain multiple information types. |
| Few-shot examples | Examples teach format and ambiguous-case judgment. Prefer examples taken from eval failures. |
| Tool use loop | Claude requests a tool call, the application executes it, returns a tool result, and calls Claude again until the model produces the final answer. |
| Message blocks | Tool-enabled APIs return structured content blocks. Applications must inspect block types instead of assuming every assistant response is final text. |
| Tool schemas | Tool names, descriptions, input schemas, field descriptions, required fields, enums, and examples all influence whether Claude selects and fills tools correctly. |
| Multiple tools | Focused tools with clear boundaries beat many overlapping tools. More tools can reduce reliability if descriptions and responsibilities blur. |
| Batch tool | Batch tools can help independent work happen together, but they should not hide dependencies or remove normal loop/error handling. |
| Text edit and web search tools | Specialized tools should be chosen by task shape. Editing tools need context and review; search tools need source evaluation and provenance. |
| RAG | Retrieval augmented generation retrieves relevant chunks instead of stuffing entire corpora into prompts. It improves grounding only when retrieval quality is good. |
| Chunking | Chunks should preserve semantic coherence and enough context to answer questions. Bad chunking creates misleading partial evidence. |
| Embeddings | Embeddings support semantic similarity, but they can miss exact identifiers, filenames, policy codes, and unusual terms. |
| BM25 and hybrid search | BM25 is strong for exact words and identifiers. Combine lexical and vector retrieval when both exact and semantic matching matter. |
| Reranking | Reranking can improve result order at additional latency/cost. Use it when first-pass retrieval finds plausible but poorly ordered chunks. |
| Contextual retrieval | Add short document-level context to chunks before indexing so retrieved chunks carry meaning outside their original location. |
| Citations | Citations and claim-source mappings support verification and uncertainty handling. Do not collapse sourced material into unsupported synthesis. |
| Prompt caching | Caching helps when large stable prompt prefixes repeat. It is a cost/latency optimization, not a correctness mechanism. |
| MCP | MCP separates clients, servers, tools, resources, and prompts. Tools are model-controlled actions; resources are app-controlled context; prompts are reusable user-invoked workflows. |
| MCP inspector | Test MCP primitives in the inspector before relying on them in Claude Code or agent workflows. |
| Claude Code setup/action | Claude Code workflows benefit from durable project context, planning before risky edits, tests, and review. Exact setup mechanics still need deeper study from Claude Code-focused material. |
| Parallel Claude Code | Use separate worktrees for parallel Claude Code sessions so independent work does not collide in one checkout. |
| Automated debugging | Claude can inspect logs and propose fixes, but production debugging needs tests, guardrails, review, and deployment controls. |
| Workflows vs agents | Use fixed workflows when the path is predictable. Use agents when the model must inspect state, choose tools, and adapt across turns. |
| Parallelization, chaining, routing | Parallelize independent subtasks, chain dependent steps, and route by task type or complexity. |
| Computer use | The course includes computer use, but the exam guide marks computer use and vision/image analysis as out of scope. Preserve only the general observe-act-tool-loop lesson. |

notes_sections.title: Decision Rules
notes_sections.body:
- If a failure occurs before the first model call on Vertex, check model access, project selection, and credentials before changing prompts.
- If a scenario asks for exam-relevant architecture, do not answer with cloud-provider setup unless the problem is explicitly access/authentication.
- If the system must remember prior turns, store and resend relevant history; do not assume Vertex or Claude stores application state.
- If output feeds software, choose tool/schema-based structured output and validation over prose formatting instructions.
- If a prompt fails on subjective quality, build representative evals and use model-based grading with calibration.
- If a format or field rule is deterministic, use code-based grading or validators rather than a model judge.
- If a tool must always run before a risky action, enforce the sequence programmatically; prompt instructions alone are weaker.
- If similar tools are confused, improve names/descriptions and clarify input/output boundaries before adding a routing layer.
- If retrieval misses exact values, add lexical/BM25 or hybrid search rather than increasing prompt length.
- If retrieved chunks lack context, improve chunking/contextual retrieval before blaming Claude.
- If users need trust in generated claims, preserve citations and claim-source mappings through synthesis.
- If work is predictable, use a workflow; if it requires environment inspection and dynamic tool choice, use an agent with guardrails.
- If Claude Code sessions run in parallel, isolate them with worktrees and merge after reviewing diffs and tests.

notes_sections.title: Anti-Patterns
notes_sections.body:
- Treating Skilljar progress state as documentation evidence. Repo completion depends on transformed study artifacts.
- Over-studying Vertex console clicks, billing, or exact provider mechanics for an exam that excludes specific cloud-provider configuration.
- Assuming `gcloud` authentication or model enablement improves prompt reliability.
- Relying on "return JSON" without schemas, validators, retries, or review.
- Using low temperature as a substitute for correctness checks.
- Treating streaming as a reliability feature instead of a UX latency feature.
- Giving Claude many overlapping tools with vague descriptions.
- Ignoring structured message blocks and parsing only assistant text.
- Using embeddings alone for exact IDs, filenames, or policy terms.
- Summarizing retrieved evidence without preserving provenance.
- Connecting MCP servers before testing tools/resources/prompts.
- Running multiple Claude Code agents in one working tree.
- Treating computer use details as exam content.

notes_sections.title: Scenario Traps
notes_sections.body:
- Trap: "The course title says Vertex, so memorize Google Cloud setup." Better: know setup as context, but study transferable Claude API, tool, RAG, MCP, prompt, and agent tradeoffs.
- Trap: "The user clicked through Skilljar, so the course is documented." Better: documentation requires notes, flashcards, practice questions, tracker updates, and progress-file updates.
- Trap: "Authentication succeeded, so the app is reliable." Better: credentials only unlock access; reliability comes from context management, validation, evals, guardrails, and error handling.
- Trap: "Streaming is the right fix for slow or wrong structured output." Better: streaming helps users see tokens sooner; schemas and validation handle structure.
- Trap: "More tools improve an agent." Better: scoped, clearly described tools reduce selection errors.
- Trap: "A model judge can grade everything." Better: deterministic checks should be code-based.
- Trap: "RAG means embeddings." Better: exact lookup often needs BM25 or hybrid retrieval.
- Trap: "MCP resources and tools are interchangeable." Better: resources expose context; tools perform model-selected actions.
- Trap: "Agents are always better than workflows." Better: workflows are simpler and more reliable when the path is known.

flashcards.question: What is the exam-relevant meaning of enabling Anthropic models in Vertex AI?
flashcards.answer: It is provider access setup; it does not replace prompt design, tool-loop logic, context management, or validation.
flashcards.example: Enabling Claude models in the Vertex Model Garden lets your app call them, but you still have to write the system prompt, structure the tool loop, and validate outputs yourself.

flashcards.question: What local setup does the readable Vertex lesson emphasize?
flashcards.answer: Install/authenticate `gcloud`, set the project ID, and configure application-default credentials so the SDK can call Vertex.
flashcards.example: Run `gcloud auth application-default login`, then `gcloud config set project my-vertex-project`, so the Claude SDK's Vertex client can pick up credentials automatically.

flashcards.question: Why should you avoid memorizing detailed Vertex console steps for the exam?
flashcards.answer: The exam guide marks specific cloud-provider configuration out of scope; study transferable Claude architecture patterns instead.
flashcards.example: Skip memorizing exact IAM role names or console screen layouts in Vertex; focus instead on prompt structure and tool-loop design, which apply the same way on Bedrock or the Anthropic API.

flashcards.question: In a multi-turn Claude app on Vertex, where does conversation state live?
flashcards.answer: In the application; the app must preserve and resend relevant prior messages.
flashcards.example: A chat app stores each turn in a database and, on every new request, resends the full prior message list to Claude, since the Vertex API itself does not remember earlier turns.

flashcards.question: What model-selection rule should guide production design?
flashcards.answer: Use the smallest, fastest, cheapest model that meets the quality bar; escalate only when capability changes outcomes.
flashcards.example: Use Haiku to classify support tickets by category, but reserve Sonnet or Opus for drafting the actual customer replies where reasoning quality matters more.

flashcards.question: What belongs in a system prompt?
flashcards.answer: Durable behavior, role, boundaries, policy, style, and output expectations.
flashcards.example: "You are a customer support agent for Acme; always respond in a friendly tone, never share internal pricing formulas, and format answers as short paragraphs."

flashcards.question: What should not be hidden in a system prompt?
flashcards.answer: Transient user facts, case-specific state, or data that should come from tools/context.
flashcards.example: Don't hardcode "the current user's name is Alex" into the system prompt; pass it in the user message or fetch it via a tool call instead.

flashcards.question: What does lower temperature improve?
flashcards.answer: Repeatability, not correctness.
flashcards.example: Setting temperature to 0 for a classification prompt makes the same input return the same label every run, but it will not fix a prompt that misclassifies a category in the first place.

flashcards.question: When is response streaming useful?
flashcards.answer: When perceived latency matters in an interactive user experience.
flashcards.example: In a chat UI, streaming tokens as they generate lets the user start reading the answer within a second instead of staring at a blank screen for the full 10-second generation.

flashcards.question: What does streaming not solve?
flashcards.answer: Schema validity, factual correctness, validation, or tool-loop control.
flashcards.example: Streaming a JSON response token by token still requires parsing and validating the final assembled JSON against your schema before you trust it.

flashcards.question: What is stronger than asking Claude to "return JSON"?
flashcards.answer: Tool/schema-based structured output plus deterministic parsing and semantic validation.
flashcards.example: Define a `record_order` tool with a strict JSON schema for fields like `item_id` and `quantity`, then have your app validate the tool call's arguments before writing to the database.

flashcards.question: When are prefill and stop sequences reasonable?
flashcards.answer: For low-risk output shaping when schema/tool enforcement is unnecessary or unavailable.
flashcards.example: Prefill the assistant turn with "{" to nudge Claude straight into JSON output for a quick internal script, where a malformed field is not a big deal.

flashcards.question: What are the core pieces of a prompt evaluation loop?
flashcards.answer: Representative test data, grading criteria, graders, and iterative prompt changes.
flashcards.example: Collect 50 real support tickets, define a rubric for "correctly identifies the issue," score each prompt version against that rubric, then tweak the prompt and re-run.

flashcards.question: When should you use model-based grading?
flashcards.answer: For semantic, subjective, completeness, or judgment-heavy criteria.
flashcards.example: Use a Claude grader to judge whether a generated email "sounds empathetic and addresses the customer's specific complaint," since no regex can check that.

flashcards.question: When should you use code-based grading?
flashcards.answer: For deterministic checks like JSON validity, required fields, regexes, arithmetic, and exact format.
flashcards.example: Write a Python assertion that checks the model's output parses as JSON and contains a non-empty `order_id` field before it's passed downstream.

flashcards.question: Why lead with a clear direct task?
flashcards.answer: It reduces inference burden and improves output consistency.
flashcards.example: Opening with "Summarize this contract in 3 bullet points" gets more consistent results than burying the actual task after several paragraphs of background context.

flashcards.question: What do examples teach beyond output format?
flashcards.answer: Ambiguous-case judgment and boundary decisions.
flashcards.example: Showing an example where a sarcastic review is labeled "negative" teaches Claude how to handle tone-based edge cases that a plain format spec wouldn't cover.

flashcards.question: Why use XML tags in prompts?
flashcards.answer: They separate instructions, examples, context, and output requirements.
flashcards.example: Wrapping reference material in `<document>...</document>` and the task in `<task>...</task>` helps Claude tell "background to read" apart from "the thing to actually do."

flashcards.question: What are the basic steps in a Claude tool-use loop?
flashcards.answer: Claude requests a tool, the app executes it, returns the tool result, then calls Claude again.
flashcards.example: Claude asks to call `get_weather(city="Seattle")`, the app runs that function, sends back "62F and rainy" as a tool_result, and Claude uses it to answer the user.

flashcards.question: What should the app inspect to decide whether to continue a tool loop?
flashcards.answer: Structured response/message block types and stop reason, not only assistant prose.
flashcards.example: Check whether `stop_reason` is `tool_use` and whether the response contains a `tool_use` content block, rather than scanning the assistant's text for phrases like "I'll call a tool now."

flashcards.question: What makes a tool schema easier for Claude to use correctly?
flashcards.answer: Clear name, description, input fields, field descriptions, required fields, enums, and boundaries.
flashcards.example: A `create_ticket` tool with a `priority` field constrained to the enum `["low","medium","high"]` and a description like "the urgency level, defaults to medium" leaves Claude no room to guess.

flashcards.question: What happens when many tools overlap?
flashcards.answer: Tool selection becomes less reliable and misrouting increases.
flashcards.example: With both `search_orders` and `search_customers` tools described almost identically, Claude may call the wrong one for a query like "find recent activity for account 123."

flashcards.question: If a tool must run before a risky action, what should enforce it?
flashcards.answer: Programmatic control flow or hooks, not prompt instructions alone.
flashcards.example: Before executing a `delete_account` tool call, the app code checks that a `confirm_deletion` tool was called first, rather than just telling Claude in the prompt "always confirm before deleting."

flashcards.question: When is a batch tool useful?
flashcards.answer: For independent operations that can run together without hidden dependencies.
flashcards.example: Fetching the current weather for five different cities at once is a good batch candidate since none of those lookups depends on another's result.

flashcards.question: What exam principle applies to text editing tools?
flashcards.answer: Inspect context before editing, make targeted changes, and verify with tests/review.
flashcards.example: Before changing a function signature, read the surrounding file to see its callers, make the minimal edit needed, then run the test suite to confirm nothing broke.

flashcards.question: What should web/search workflows preserve?
flashcards.answer: Source provenance, dates when relevant, and claim-source mappings.
flashcards.example: When Claude states "the API rate limit is 1000 requests/min," the workflow should retain which page and publish date that figure came from, in case the docs have since changed.

flashcards.question: What problem does RAG solve?
flashcards.answer: It retrieves relevant source chunks instead of sending an entire corpus to the model.
flashcards.example: Instead of pasting a 2,000-page policy manual into every prompt, RAG retrieves just the 3 paragraphs about "vacation carryover" that answer the user's question.

flashcards.question: What makes chunking good?
flashcards.answer: Chunks preserve semantic coherence and enough context to be useful when retrieved.
flashcards.example: Splitting a manual by section headings keeps a full policy explanation together, instead of cutting it mid-sentence at a fixed 500-character boundary.

flashcards.question: What are embeddings best at?
flashcards.answer: Semantic similarity.
flashcards.example: A query for "how do I get my money back" retrieves a chunk titled "Refund Policy" via embeddings even though the words don't literally match.

flashcards.question: What is BM25 best at?
flashcards.answer: Exact terms, identifiers, policy names, filenames, and codes.
flashcards.example: A search for error code "ERR_4092" reliably surfaces the exact matching document with BM25, where an embedding search might rank it lower amid semantically similar but wrong results.

flashcards.question: When should you combine BM25 and embeddings?
flashcards.answer: When queries need both exact matching and semantic matching.
flashcards.example: A support search combining BM25 and embeddings can correctly handle both "SKU-88213 return policy" (exact code) and "can I send this back" (semantic paraphrase) in the same system.

flashcards.question: When should you use reranking?
flashcards.answer: When first-pass retrieval finds plausible chunks but orders them poorly.
flashcards.example: Initial retrieval returns 20 loosely relevant chunks; a reranker then reorders them so the one directly answering the user's question lands at the top before being sent to Claude.

flashcards.question: What does contextual retrieval add?
flashcards.answer: Short document-level context to chunks before indexing so retrieved chunks remain meaningful.
flashcards.example: Prepending "This chunk is from the Q3 2024 earnings call transcript" to an isolated paragraph keeps it interpretable even after it's been split away from the rest of the document.

flashcards.question: Why are citations exam-relevant?
flashcards.answer: They support verification, provenance, uncertainty handling, and trustworthy synthesis.
flashcards.example: A generated answer that says "returns are allowed within 30 days [Source: Return Policy, p.2]" lets a user or reviewer quickly check the claim against the original document.

flashcards.question: What is prompt caching good for?
flashcards.answer: Reducing latency/cost when large stable prompt prefixes repeat.
flashcards.example: Caching a 20-page product manual that's reused as context across hundreds of customer support queries avoids reprocessing it from scratch on every request.

flashcards.question: What is prompt caching not?
flashcards.answer: A correctness or reliability mechanism.
flashcards.example: Caching a flawed system prompt just makes the same wrong behavior repeat faster and cheaper; it does nothing to fix the underlying error.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between MCP tools and resources?
flashcards.answer: Tools are model-controlled actions; resources are app-controlled context.
flashcards.example: An MCP `send_email` tool is something Claude decides to invoke mid-conversation, while an MCP resource exposing a company's style guide is context the app chooses to attach up front.

flashcards.question: What are MCP prompts?
flashcards.answer: Reusable user-invoked templates/workflows exposed by an MCP server.
flashcards.example: A `/summarize-pr` prompt exposed by a GitHub MCP server lets a user trigger a preset "review this pull request and summarize the changes" workflow with one command.

flashcards.question: Why use the MCP inspector?
flashcards.answer: To test tools, resources, and prompts before connecting them to production workflows.
flashcards.example: Run the MCP inspector against a new `search_inventory` tool to confirm it returns correctly shaped results before wiring it into the live support agent.

flashcards.question: What workflow pattern makes Claude Code safer?
flashcards.answer: Provide project context, plan before risky edits, test changes, and review diffs.
flashcards.example: Before asking Claude Code to refactor the auth module, point it at the relevant files, have it propose a plan first, then run the test suite and review the diff before merging.

flashcards.question: How should parallel Claude Code sessions be isolated?
flashcards.answer: Use separate git worktrees.
flashcards.example: Running two Claude Code sessions on the same feature branch in one working directory would clash; separate worktrees let each session edit files without stepping on the other.

flashcards.question: What guardrails should surround automated debugging?
flashcards.answer: Tests, review, limited permissions, observability, and deployment controls.
flashcards.example: Let an automated debugging agent read logs and propose a fix, but require it to run in a sandboxed branch with no direct production deploy access, and require a human to approve the merge.

flashcards.question: When should you prefer a fixed workflow?
flashcards.answer: When the path is predictable and reliability/control matter.
flashcards.example: A fixed workflow that always extracts fields, then validates, then writes to a database fits an invoice-processing pipeline where the steps never change.

flashcards.question: When should you prefer an agent?
flashcards.answer: When the system must inspect state, choose tools, and adapt dynamically.
flashcards.example: A research assistant that decides on the fly whether to search the web, query a database, or ask a clarifying question needs agent-style flexibility, not a fixed script.

flashcards.question: Match the workflow pattern to the situation: parallelization, chaining, routing.
flashcards.answer: Parallelize independent tasks, chain dependent steps, route by task type or complexity.
flashcards.example: Summarize five unrelated documents in parallel, chain "extract data -> validate -> format report" as sequential steps, and route simple FAQs to Haiku while complex ones go to Opus.

flashcards.question: How should computer use be treated for this exam?
flashcards.answer: Out of scope except as broad observe-act-tool-loop context.
flashcards.example: Know that computer use lets Claude view a screenshot and click/type like a user in a general observe-decide-act loop, but don't expect exam questions on specific screen-coordinate APIs.

practice_questions.scenario: A team can call Claude successfully through Vertex AI after enabling Anthropic models and configuring `gcloud`. Their structured extraction app still sometimes returns malformed JSON that breaks downstream parsing.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best next design change?

choices.text: Re-run `gcloud auth application-default login` before each extraction request.
Lower temperature to zero and keep asking for JSON in the prompt.
Use schema/tool-based structured output with deterministic parsing and validation.
Switch from Vertex AI to another provider because provider setup caused the malformed output.

practice_questions.explanation: Provider authentication only enables access. Machine-consumed output needs schema enforcement, parsing, validation, and retry/review patterns.

distractors.A: Authentication does not enforce output shape.
distractors.B: Low temperature improves repeatability but does not guarantee valid or semantically correct JSON.
distractors.D: The failure is output-control design, not necessarily provider choice.

practice_questions.scenario: A Vertex-hosted chatbot loses track of a customer's previous order number after several turns. Logs show each request sends only the latest user message.
practice_questions.prompt: What should the application change?

choices.text: Store and resend relevant conversation history with each request.
Increase temperature so Claude can infer missing details.
Enable the model again in Vertex AI Model Garden.
Use streaming so earlier tokens are visible sooner.

practice_questions.explanation: Conversation state is application-managed. The app must supply relevant prior user, assistant, and tool messages.

distractors.B: Higher temperature worsens repeatability and does not recover missing context.
distractors.C: Model access is already working.
distractors.D: Streaming affects latency, not memory.

practice_questions.scenario: An exam scenario mentions Google Cloud setup details, but the failure is that a customer-support agent refunds users before verifying identity.
practice_questions.prompt: Which fix best matches the certification's tested architecture judgment?

choices.text: Add a note in the Vertex setup guide reminding engineers to verify customers.
Enforce the verification step programmatically before refund tools can run.
Increase the model's context window so it remembers the policy.
Use a faster model so the agent checks identity sooner.

practice_questions.explanation: Required business sequences need deterministic enforcement. Prompt-only or documentation-only approaches are weaker when mistakes have financial impact.

distractors.A: Documentation does not enforce runtime behavior.
distractors.C: More context does not guarantee sequence compliance.
distractors.D: Speed does not enforce policy.

practice_questions.scenario: A prompt evaluation suite checks whether generated JSON parses, contains required fields, and uses valid enum values.
practice_questions.prompt: Which grading approach is best for these checks?

choices.text: Model-based grading with a general rubric.
Code-based grading with deterministic validators.
Human review of every output before running tests.
Reranking outputs by likely quality.

practice_questions.explanation: Parseability, required fields, and enum membership are objective and should be checked deterministically.

distractors.A: Model judges are better for semantic quality, not exact validity.
distractors.C: Human review is too slow for deterministic checks.
distractors.D: Reranking is a retrieval technique, not an output validator.

practice_questions.scenario: A documentation assistant uses embeddings for RAG but fails whenever users search exact policy IDs and ticket numbers.
practice_questions.prompt: What should you add first?

choices.text: BM25 or another lexical retrieval path, then combine it with semantic retrieval.
Prompt caching for the full document corpus.
Higher temperature to improve recall.
A longer system prompt listing every policy ID.

practice_questions.explanation: Exact identifiers are a lexical-search strength. Hybrid retrieval handles both exact and semantic matching.

distractors.B: Prompt caching optimizes repeated prompt prefixes, not retrieval accuracy.
distractors.C: Temperature does not fix missing retrieval.
distractors.D: Listing every ID in the system prompt is brittle and wastes context.

practice_questions.scenario: An MCP server exposes `lookup_customer`, `get_order`, and `refund_order`. Claude often chooses the wrong lookup tool because descriptions are one sentence each and boundaries overlap.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the most effective first improvement?

choices.text: Give Claude access to more tools so it has alternatives.
Improve tool names/descriptions, input schemas, examples, and boundary conditions.
Disable all tools and ask the user to paste data manually.
Move the MCP server from project scope to user scope.

practice_questions.explanation: Tool descriptions and schemas are the primary signals for tool selection. Clear boundaries reduce misrouting.

distractors.A: More overlapping tools usually worsens selection.
distractors.C: This avoids the integration instead of fixing it.
distractors.D: Scope does not address ambiguous tool semantics.

practice_questions.scenario: A synthesis agent needs verified source claims from RAG results. Current summaries omit source URLs and page references, making audit impossible.
practice_questions.prompt: What should upstream retrieval/summarization produce?

choices.text: Longer natural-language summaries without citations.
Structured claim-source mappings that downstream synthesis must preserve.
A cached prompt prefix with all document names.
A single confidence score without evidence.

practice_questions.explanation: Provenance requires structured source metadata attached to claims, not unsupported summaries.

distractors.A: Length does not guarantee provenance.
distractors.C: Caching is not evidence tracking.
distractors.D: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and not auditable.

practice_questions.scenario: A workflow asks Claude to run three independent compliance checks over the same document, then combine the results.
practice_questions.prompt: Which architecture pattern fits best?

choices.text: Parallelization for the independent checks, followed by synthesis.
Chaining all checks in a fixed sequence even though none depend on another.
Routing to only one checker based on document length.
A Vertex setup retry loop before each check.

practice_questions.explanation: Independent subtasks can run in parallel, then be synthesized after all results are available.

distractors.B: Chaining adds unnecessary latency for independent work.
distractors.C: Routing chooses one path; the scenario needs all checks.
distractors.D: Provider setup is unrelated to decomposition.

practice_questions.scenario: A process has a predictable three-step path: extract metadata, validate fields, then enrich valid records. The team wants the simplest reliable design.
practice_questions.prompt: What should they prefer?

choices.text: A fixed chained workflow with validation gates.
A fully autonomous agent that decides whether validation is needed.
A high-temperature prompt that encourages creativity.
A web search tool for every record.

practice_questions.explanation: Known sequences are good fits for workflows. Validation gates provide control and predictability.

distractors.B: An agent adds unnecessary variability when the path is known.
distractors.C: Creativity is not useful for deterministic processing.
distractors.D: Search is irrelevant unless enrichment requires external lookup.

practice_questions.scenario: Two Claude Code sessions need to implement unrelated features in the same repository at the same time.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the safest workspace setup?

choices.text: Run both sessions in the same checkout and resolve conflicts later.
Use separate git worktrees and merge after reviewing diffs and tests.
Ask both sessions to avoid editing the same files without checking.
Disable tests until both sessions finish.

practice_questions.explanation: Worktrees isolate parallel edits and make review/merge boundaries explicit.

distractors.A: Shared checkouts increase accidental collisions.
distractors.C: Prompt instructions do not reliably prevent file conflicts.
distractors.D: Tests are needed to verify independent work before merge.

practice_questions.scenario: A team uses an MCP server to expose a large document catalog. Claude repeatedly calls exploratory search tools just to discover what documents exist.
practice_questions.prompt: What MCP primitive should the server add?

choices.text: A resource that exposes a catalog or hierarchy of available documents.
A refund tool with a broader schema.
A prompt caching rule for every user question.
A forced final-answer tool.

practice_questions.explanation: MCP resources expose app-controlled context and catalogs, reducing unnecessary exploratory tool calls.

distractors.B: Unrelated action tools do not improve catalog visibility.
distractors.C: Caching does not reveal available documents.
distractors.D: Forced final answers do not supply context.
